notes.h: Planning a comparative study (Higher Level only)
notes.b: A comparative evaluation tests whether one preserved food is better than another, so the test must be fair and the criteria must be set in advance.
points: Choose one food that can be preserved by two methods, such as strawberries frozen and strawberries made into jam.
Use sound, ripe fruit from the same batch for both methods, so differences come from the preservation method rather than the raw material.
Compare the same criteria for each method: nutritional value, sensory qualities, safety, storage life, time, energy and packaging.
State the underlying principle of each method and the risk of spoilage that each carries.
Conclude by judging which method suits the stated purpose, weighing its advantages against its disadvantages.

notes.h: Nutritional comparison: freezing and canning (Higher Level only)
points: Freezing keeps more vitamin C than canning, because canning uses higher temperatures for longer.
Water-soluble vitamins, such as vitamin C and the B group, leach into blanching water and canning liquid, and are lost when the liquid is drained away.
Thiamine (vitamin B1) is heat-sensitive, so the high temperatures of canning destroy much of it.
Sample data for practice: vitamin C in peas was 25 mg when fresh, 17 mg after freezing and 8 mg after canning.
Sample data for practice: sodium in peas was 1 mg when fresh and 230 mg after canning, because salt is added during canning.

notes.h: Sensory and nutritional comparison: frozen strawberries and jam (Higher Level only)
points: Frozen strawberries keep their colour and flavour closer to those of fresh fruit.
Thawed frozen strawberries are softer and release juice, because ice crystals have damaged the cell walls.
Jam is sweeter, darker from cooking, and firmer and spreadable in texture.
Jam loses some heat-sensitive vitamin C during boiling, whereas frozen fruit retains more.
Jam's high sugar content makes it unsuitable for people restricting their sugar intake.

notes.h: Risk of spoilage in each method (Higher Level only)
points: Frozen fruit is not sterile: if the temperature fluctuates, partial thawing releases moisture, and surviving micro-organisms can grow.
Freezer burn occurs when air reaches the food through loose or damaged packs, causing drying, toughening and discolouration by oxidation.
Thawed fruit should be used promptly and never refrozen.
Jam spoils by fermentation or mould growth when the sugar is too low, setting point is not reached, jars are not clean, or the seal fails.
A bulging lid, gas, mould or an off-odour in a jar means the jam must be discarded.

notes.h: Energy, cost and environmental factors (Higher Level only)
points: Freezing needs a continuous electricity supply and freezer space; jam needs no freezer but needs fuel for cooking.
Sealed jam keeps well without a freezer and has a long shelf life when stored in a cool, dark place.
Low-acid vegetables such as peas must be pressure canned, because boiling water does not destroy the spores of Clostridium botulinum.
Glass jars can be washed and reused or recycled; plastic freezer bags are usually made from non-renewable oil and are hard to recycle.

keyTerms.definition: A structured comparison of two or more preserved foods or methods against set criteria, leading to a judgement on suitability.
The features of food perceived by the senses, such as colour, flavour, aroma and texture.
A vitamin that dissolves in water, such as vitamin C or a B vitamin, and is lost in cooking water or drained liquid.
A solution of salt in water used to preserve or pack food, which raises the sodium content of the food.
Processing sealed jars in a pressure cooker at a temperature above boiling point, which is needed to destroy the spores in low-acid foods.
Drying, toughening and discolouration of frozen food caused by air reaching the surface through loose or damaged packaging.
A chemical reaction with oxygen that causes discolouration, loss of flavour and rancidity in food.

questions.prompt: Name one nutritional difference between frozen and canned vegetables and explain the reason for it.
questions.model: Vitamin C: canned vegetables lose more vitamin C than frozen ones, because canning uses high temperatures for longer, and the vitamin dissolves into the liquid that is drained away. Alternative answer: canned vegetables contain more sodium than frozen ones, because salt is added during canning.

questions.prompt: Plan and evaluate a comparison between two preserved versions of the same food, covering the criteria you would use, how you would keep the test fair, the spoilage risks of each method and a final judgement.
questions.model: Food and methods: one fruit, such as strawberries, preserved by freezing and by jam making. Fair test: the same sound, ripe batch of fruit is used for both methods, and the same criteria are compared. Criteria: nutritional value (vitamin C loss in jam from boiling; retention in frozen fruit), sensory qualities (frozen fruit closer to fresh colour and flavour; jam sweeter, darker and firmer), safety, storage life, time, energy and packaging. Principles: freezing removes heat and makes water unavailable, with blanching only for vegetables; jam uses heat, a concentrated sugar solution by osmosis, pectin and acid, and a sealed jar. Spoilage risks: frozen fruit is not sterile and can spoil after partial thawing or fluctuating temperature, and freezer burn follows loose packs; jam can ferment or grow mould if sugar is too low, setting point is not reached, jars are unclean or the seal fails. Judgement: freezing suits fresh-tasting fruit for desserts and is the better choice where a freezer is available and the fruit is to be used soon after thawing; jam suits long storage without a freezer, though it has a high sugar content and more loss of fresh qualities. The judgement must state which method suits the stated purpose and why.
